This is a problem because a simple word substitution isn't enough to fix the sentence correctly, and it needs to be restructured instead.
ste-practices.word-swap-insufficient.fine_when: It is acceptable if, after substituting the replacement word, the sentence remains grammatical, meaningful, and still carries the original meaning.

ste-procedural.condition-after-command.catches: This flags instructions where the condition comes after the command instead of before it. Reading the command first before knowing the condition that governs it can make instructions harder to follow.

ste-procedural.instruction-not-imperativ.catches: This rule flags an instruction step that is phrased as a description or obligation statement instead of a direct command, such as naming a subject with a modal like "must" or "should," or using an impersonal opener like "it is necessary to." This is a problem because instructions should tell the reader exactly what to do rather than describe what should happen.
ste-procedural.instruction-not-imperativ.fine_when: This phrasing is acceptable inside a note, since notes are meant to be descriptive rather than imperative.

ste-procedural.multiple-instructions-per.catches: This flags a step written as one sentence that actually contains more than one instruction. That's a problem because a reader may only follow one of the instructions or lose track of the order they need to happen in.
ste-procedural.multiple-instructions-per.fine_when: It is acceptable when the two actions described happen at the same time, since the rule allows two actions in one sentence in that case.

ste-procedural.note-gives-instruction.catches: This flags a note that contains an instruction (a command telling the reader to do something) rather than plain information. This is a problem because readers often skip notes, so an instruction placed there may never be seen or followed.
ste-procedural.note-gives-instruction.fine_when: It is acceptable when the instruction is moved before the note marker (as a step) and the note itself only states information, not a command.

ste-procedural.sentence-too-long-procedu.catches: This rule flags an instruction that is longer than twenty words. A long instruction is hard for a reader to follow, so it should be split into separate numbered steps.

ste-punctuation.colon-terminates-sentenc.catches: This flags a list lead-in (the text before a colon introducing a list) that has too many words, based on the same word-count cap used for sentence length. A long lead-in makes the reader hold too much information before they even get to the list items.

ste-punctuation.hyphen-group-too-long.catches: You flag hyphenated word groups that chain together more than three words. Long hyphen chains like this can be hard for a reader to parse and understand.
ste-punctuation.hyphen-group-too-long.fine_when: It is acceptable when the hyphenated group is a package name, CSS class, or Kubernetes resource name, or otherwise registered as a domain term.

ste-punctuation.hyphen-missing-in-compou.catches: You flag two words acting together as a single descriptive term before a noun when they are written as separate words instead of joined by a hyphen. Without the hyphen, a reader may momentarily misread the two words as separate ideas rather than one combined description.

ste-punctuation.parentheses-misuse.catches: This flags a parenthetical that carries a second idea instead of serving one of the allowed purposes (cross-reference, item identifier, step number, abbreviation, singular-and-plural form, short explanation, or alternative). This is a problem because it hides an extra idea inside parentheses instead of giving it its own sentence, making the text harder to read.
ste-punctuation.parentheses-misuse.fine_when: It's acceptable when the parenthetical gives a cross-reference, an item identifier, a step number, an abbreviation, a singular-and-plural form, a short explanation, or an alternative.

ste-punctuation.semicolon-used.catches: You flag any use of a semicolon in a sentence. Semicolons let sentences run on too long and can be used incorrectly, making the text harder to follow.
ste-punctuation.semicolon-used.fine_when: This does not apply when the semicolon appears inside a code span, such as shell commands, CSS, SQL, or PATH values.

ste-safety.risk-level-word-missing-or-wr.catches: This flags text where the risk marker used doesn't match how serious the actual consequence is, such as using a lower-level word when the risk is unrecoverable data loss or a security exposure, or missing a marker entirely. This matters because a reader may not take the right precautions if the warning understates or omits the real danger.

ste-safety.safety-block-does-not-start-w.catches: This flags a safety block (like a warning or caution) that opens with a description of the risk instead of the command to run or the condition to watch for. This is a problem because a reader who only reads the first sentence would not know what action to take.

ste-safety.safety-block-missing-conseque.catches: This rule flags a safety warning that tells you not to do something but never explains what will happen if you do it anyway. Without that explanation, you have no way to judge how serious the risk is or why you should care.

ste-sentences.complex-text-not-in-vertic.catches: This flags a sentence that packs a large number of coordinated items into a single inline list. Reading many items strung together in a sentence is hard to follow, so the rule suggests breaking them out into a vertical list instead.
ste-sentences.complex-text-not-in-vertic.fine_when: It's acceptable when the sentence has only a few coordinated items, since a small number of items still reads cleanly inline.

ste-sentences.missing-article-or-determi.catches: This rule flags a noun that appears right after a sentence-initial verb without an article or demonstrative like "the," "a," "an," "this," or "these" in front of it. This is a problem for a reader because the sentence can read as unclear or incomplete without a word marking which or how many of the noun is meant.
ste-sentences.missing-article-or-determi.fine_when: It is acceptable when the noun is in subject position rather than following a sentence-initial verb, when the statement is general, when it refers to an abstract quality, when the noun is followed by an alphanumeric identifier, or when the text is a heading.

ste-sentences.missing-connector-between-.catches: This flags two consecutive sentences where the second adds a result, contrast, or next step to the first, but no connecting word or phrase makes that relationship clear. Without the connection spelled out, the reader has to guess how the two sentences relate to each other.
ste-sentences.missing-connector-between-.fine_when: It is acceptable if the second sentence does not actually add a result, a contrast, or a next step to the first.

ste-sentences.omitted-word-or-contractio.catches: This flags contractions (like "don't" or "it's") and sentences that leave out a subject or article, such as starting a conditional with "If configured," instead of "If it is configured,". These omissions can make sentences ambiguous or less precise about who or what is being referred to.

ste-sentences.sentence-not-short-or-clea.catches: This rule flags sentences that try to give more than one instruction or cover more than one topic at once. Cramming multiple instructions or topics into a single sentence makes it harder for the reader to follow and act on.

ste-sentences.vertical-list-item-punctua.catches: This flags list items that aren't punctuated consistently, such as items not starting with a capital letter, items ending in commas or semicolons instead of appropriate punctuation, or the last item missing a final period. Inconsistent punctuation across list items can make a list harder to read and looks unpolished.

ste-sentences.vertical-list-lead-in-miss.catches: This rule flags a sentence introducing a vertical list when that sentence ends with a period instead of a colon. This is a problem because the lead-in should signal to the reader that a list follows.

ste-verbs.auxiliary-stacking.catches: This flags sentences that stack multiple auxiliary verbs together (such as 'will have been' or 'has to be') instead of stating the action plainly. This kind of phrasing buries the actual action and makes the sentence harder to read and act on.
ste-verbs.auxiliary-stacking.fine_when: A modal followed directly by a bare verb (like 'you must rotate the token') is permitted and not flagged.

ste-verbs.complex-tense.catches: This rule flags verb constructions that use perfect tenses (have/has plus a participle), progressive tenses (is/are plus -ing), or future perfect tense, instead of simple present, past, or future tense. This is a problem for a reader because these complex verb forms can make sentences harder to read than necessary when a simpler tense would express the same meaning.
ste-verbs.complex-tense.fine_when: This is acceptable in changelog entries, since release notes conventionally use the present perfect tense for describing shipped changes, and in status reports covering completion and status statements that use the same tense legitimately.

ste-verbs.gerund-outside-noun-use.catches: This flags an -ing word that is doing the work of the main verb in a sentence instead of acting as a noun or a noun modifier. When an -ing form carries the action of the clause, it can make the sentence unclear or harder to follow, and the rule asks you to rewrite it with a finite verb or split it into its own sentence.
ste-verbs.gerund-outside-noun-use.fine_when: It is acceptable when the -ing word is a noun (naming a thing or process) or is part of a noun as a modifier, including cases inside quotations, code spans, or registered domain terms.

ste-verbs.nominalized-action.catches: This flags sentences that turn an action into a noun paired with a light verb (like 'performs a validation of' or 'provides protection against') instead of using the action's verb directly. This pattern makes writing wordier and less direct than it needs to be.
ste-verbs.nominalized-action.fine_when: This is acceptable for the phrase 'do a test,' since the noun form of 'test' is permitted while the verb form is not.

ste-verbs.passive-voice.catches: This rule flags sentences written in the passive voice, where the subject receives the action instead of performing it. This is a problem because it can leave the actor unnamed, making the sentence less direct and clear.
ste-verbs.passive-voice.fine_when: The passive voice is acceptable in descriptive text when the actor is genuinely unknown.

ste-verbs.past-participle-not-adjectival.catches: This flags a past participle that is being used as part of a verb construction (sitting after an auxiliary other than "be", "become", or "stay") rather than as an adjective. This can make a sentence rely on passive or complex verb forms instead of clearly stating who or what is performing the action.
ste-verbs.past-participle-not-adjectival.fine_when: It is acceptable when the past participle sits before a noun it describes, or when it follows a form of "be", "become", or "stay" to describe a condition.

ste-verbs.verb-form-not-listed.catches: This flags a verb form that is not one of the accepted forms of its base verb, which can make the writing inconsistent with the expected style or harder to follow.

ste-words.approved-word-substitution.catches: The rule flags a word from a specific list and asks you to swap it for a designated replacement word instead. This matters because the original word is considered inconsistent, even though readers would still understand it.
ste-words.approved-word-substitution.fine_when: The rule is treated as advisory rather than mandatory, since the flagged word is understood by readers and only creates inconsistency, not a comprehension problem.

ste-words.domain-noun-category-membershi.catches: This flags a noun that is not in the controlled vocabulary and does not clearly name a concept in one of the project's declared domain-noun categories. This is a problem because the reader cannot tell what the noun refers to or confirm it is a legitimate project term.
ste-words.domain-noun-category-membershi.fine_when: It is acceptable when the noun, though outside the controlled vocabulary, does name a specified concept that falls within one of the declared domain-noun categories for the project.

ste-words.domain-noun-not-organization-a.catches: This flags when you use a different word for something that your project's glossary, API reference, or schema already names. It's a problem because readers may not realize you're referring to the same thing, or may get confused by inconsistent terminology.
ste-words.domain-noun-not-organization-a.fine_when: It's acceptable if the project's glossary, API reference, or schema does not already define a name for the thing being described.

ste-words.domain-noun-too-long-or-unclea.catches: This flags a newly invented domain term that is longer than three words or that a reader outside your team wouldn't understand without a definition. Such terms make the text harder to follow because readers can't easily grasp their meaning.
ste-words.domain-noun-too-long-or-unclea.fine_when: It is fine if the term is three words or fewer and a reader outside your team would understand it without needing a definition.

ste-words.domain-verb-category-membershi.catches: This flags a verb that is not one of the standard vocabulary verbs, used in a sentence that could have been written with an ordinary vocabulary verb instead, or used without belonging to a declared domain-verb category with its category meaning intact. This is a problem because it introduces a non-standard word where plain wording would work, or uses a specialized term outside the meaning it's supposed to carry.
ste-words.domain-verb-category-membershi.fine_when: It is acceptable if the sentence could not be written with vocabulary verbs alone, and the verb belongs to a declared domain-verb category and carries that category's meaning in the sentence.

ste-words.inconsistent-term-for-same-thi.catches: This flags a document that refers to the same thing using two different terms, such as calling something one name in one sentence and a different name later. That is a problem because it forces you to figure out whether the two terms mean the same thing or something different, which slows down and confuses reading.
ste-words.inconsistent-term-for-same-thi.fine_when: The rule can only be checked reliably when a list of known synonym groups is available to confirm that two terms actually refer to the same thing; without such a list, it cannot be determined that the terms are truly interchangeable.

ste-words.noun-used-as-verb.catches: This flags a domain noun that is being used as a verb, and asks you to use a real verb instead while keeping the noun as a noun. Using the noun this way can make the writing less clear or less standard.
ste-words.noun-used-as-verb.fine_when: This rule only applies to a specific, short list of nouns chosen because their verb use is common in software writing and can be cleanly replaced; other nouns used as verbs, such as "log" or "build," are not covered by this rule.

ste-words.obligation-word-substitution.catches: This flags inconsistent use of different obligation words (like 'should', 'shall', 'must') for expressing the same kind of requirement. Mixing these words can make it unclear whether something is truly required or just recommended.
ste-words.obligation-word-substitution.fine_when: A document that uses 'should' consistently throughout is still understood, and outside of a specification the choice between obligation words is a matter of consistency rather than an actual defect.

ste-words.slang-or-jargon-term.catches: This rule flags slang or jargon words used as if they were precise technical terms. This is a problem because readers may not understand casual or informal terms, or may interpret them inconsistently, instead of getting a clear description of the actual behavior.

ste-words.spelling.catches: You flag words spelled in a non-American English way, since the text should use en-US spelling instead. Inconsistent spelling conventions can make the text look unpolished or unclear about which regional standard it follows.

ste-words.unapproved-word-not-a-domain-n.catches: This flags a word that isn't in the approved vocabulary list when that word is not a domain-specific term (or part of one). Such a word is a problem because it should be replaced rather than kept as-is.
ste-words.unapproved-word-not-a-domain-n.fine_when: It is acceptable when the out-of-vocabulary word is a domain noun, or is a word inside a multi-word domain noun.

ste-words.verb-or-adjective-form-not-per.catches: This rule flags a word form that is not one of the allowed forms of its base word (for example, an inflected verb or adjective form outside the permitted set). Such a form is a problem for a reader because it is not a recognized or accepted way to write that word, which can make the sentence confusing or nonstandard.

ste-words.verb-used-as-noun.catches: You flag using a verb from a specific set as if it were a noun (for example, saying 'the deploy' instead of 'the deployment'). This is a problem because it uses a non-standard word form where a proper noun form exists.

ste-words.word-outside-controlled-vocabu.catches: This rule flags any word that the project has put on its own blocklist. Using such a word is a problem because the project has specifically said this word should not appear, and a replacement or rewrite is expected instead.
ste-words.word-outside-controlled-vocabu.fine_when: There is no stated case in the definition where a blocklisted word is acceptable.

ste-words.word-used-in-wrong-part-of-spe.catches: This flags a word that is being used as a part of speech (for example, a verb) that isn't the part of speech it's permitted to have (for example, a noun). This is a problem because it uses the word in a way that isn't allowed for it, even though the word itself is otherwise acceptable.

ste-words.word-used-outside-permitted-se.catches: This flags a controlled word that is being used with a different meaning than the one meaning it's allowed to carry. This is a problem because a reader may understand the word in its ordinary dictionary sense when only one specific, defined meaning is intended.
ste-words.word-used-outside-permitted-se.fine_when: It is acceptable when the word is used to carry exactly the single meaning recorded for it, even if the word also has other dictionary meanings.
